sections.overview: The Greater Short-toed Lark is a small migrant breeding in open warm regions of southern Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, then wintering farther south.
sections.identification: At about 13–14 cm, it has sandy streaked upperparts, pale underparts, a short conical bill and dark breast-side spots; it lacks the Skylark’s crest.
sections.habitat: It favours warm, dry open ground with sparse low vegetation and bare patches, including steppe, sandy or stony fields and fallow land.
sections.diet: It forages on the ground for seeds and small invertebrates, taking more insect prey in breeding season.
sections.behavior: It occurs in pairs while breeding and gathers into flocks during migration and winter, sometimes with other larks.
sections.reproduction: It nests in a shallow ground scrape concealed among sparse vegetation; brood number varies with conditions.
sections.ecology: It is compared with the Lesser Short-toed Lark (Alaudala rufescens, formerly Calandrella): this species has a larger bill and less breast streaking, and may resemble Alauda arvensis.
sections.conservation: It is globally Least Concern, though conversion and intensification of dry open grasslands can remove habitat locally.
